front: How did WWI impact Germany?
p1: British naval blockade → mass starvation — 750,000 civilian deaths.
p2: 2 million German soldiers killed; war trebled government debts.
p3: Collapse of law and order - Kiel Mutiny saw sailors refusing to follow orders.
s: British naval blockade → mass starvation — 750,000 civilian deaths.
2 million German soldiers killed; war trebled government debts.
Collapse of law and order - Kiel Mutiny saw sailors refusing to follow orders.

front: What happened in November 1918?
p1: Kaiser Wilhelm had lost control over the army and there was a collapse of law and order by late 1918.
p2: Wilhelm abdicated 9 November 1918; Weimar Republic declared the same day by leading politicians.
p3: Armistice signed 11 November 1918 — over 11 million Germans had served; 2 million died. No Allied soldier had entered Germany → 'stab-in-the-back' myth began.
s: Kaiser Wilhelm had lost control over the army and there was a collapse of law and order by late 1918.
Wilhelm abdicated 9 November 1918; Weimar Republic declared the same day by leading politicians.
Armistice signed 11 November 1918 — over 11 million Germans had served; 2 million died. No Allied soldier had entered Germany → 'stab-in-the-back' myth began.

front: How did the Weimar Republic begin?
p1: Ebert emerged as dominant politician Nov 1918–Jul 1919, reassuring the army and industrialists that communism would not take hold.
p2: Defeated the Spartacist uprising, proving he could maintain order.
p3: Weimar Constitution agreed July 1919: President (head of state, elected every 7 years), Chancellor (day-to-day government), Reichstag (directly elected parliament).
s: Ebert emerged as dominant politician Nov 1918–Jul 1919, reassuring the army and industrialists that communism would not take hold.
Defeated the Spartacist uprising, proving he could maintain order.
Weimar Constitution agreed July 1919: President (head of state, elected every 7 years), Chancellor (day-to-day government), Reichstag (directly elected parliament).

front: What happened during the Spartacist Revolt?
p1: January 1919: communist Spartacists led by Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht attempted to seize power.
p2: 100,000 workers struck in Berlin and seized government communication offices.
p3: Ebert sent in Freikorps (far-right ex-soldiers) who crushed the revolt; Luxemburg and Liebknecht were killed.

100,000 workers struck in Berlin and seized government communication offices.
Ebert sent in Freikorps (far-right ex-soldiers) who crushed the revolt; Luxemburg and Liebknecht were killed.

front: What happened during the Kapp Putsch?
p1: March 1920: Ebert tried to disband the Freikorps; Wolfgang Kapp led 5,000 armed men in a march on Berlin.
p2: Government fled to Stuttgart; called for passive resistance → workers went on strike.
p3: Kapp could not govern and fled after four days; rebellion collapsed.
s: March 1920: Ebert tried to disband the Freikorps; Wolfgang Kapp led 5,000 armed men in a march on Berlin.
Government fled to Stuttgart; called for passive resistance → workers went on strike.
Kapp could not govern and fled after four days; rebellion collapsed.

front: What were the weaknesses of the Weimar Constitution?
p1: Article 48 allowed laws to be passed without the Reichstag in an emergency.
p2: Proportional representation → 9 unstable coalition governments 1919–23.
p3: The Weimar Republic was created out of violence in the aftermath of WWI. Violence was always seen as an acceptable part of politics in Germany.
s: Article 48 allowed laws to be passed without the Reichstag in an emergency.
Proportional representation → 9 unstable coalition governments 1919–23.
The Weimar Republic was created out of violence in the aftermath of WWI. Violence was always seen as an acceptable part of politics in Germany.

front: What were the strengths of the Weimar Constitution?
p1: All men and women had equal voting rights.
p2: Power was divided between the President, Chancellor, and Reichstag to avoid one person having too much power.
p3: Proportional Representation: every vote had equal weight; any party winning 60,000 votes gained a Reichstag seat.

Power was divided between the President, Chancellor, and Reichstag to avoid one person having too much power.
Proportional Representation: every vote had equal weight; any party winning 60,000 votes gained a Reichstag seat.

front: What were the terms of the Treaty of Versailles?
p1: Army limited to 100,000 men; no air force; navy severely restricted. Rhineland on border with France demilitarised.
p2: Germany lost 13% of land including Alsace-Lorraine (to France), all colonies, and the Polish Corridor.
p3: War Guilt Clause (Article 231) forced Germany to accept 100% of the blame for WWI. Had to pay £6.6 billion reparations.
s: Army limited to 100,000 men; no air force; navy severely restricted. Rhineland on border with France demilitarised.
Germany lost 13% of land including Alsace-Lorraine (to France), all colonies, and the Polish Corridor.
War Guilt Clause (Article 231) forced Germany to accept 100% of the blame for WWI. Had to pay £6.6 billion reparations.

front: How did Germans react to the Treaty of Versailles?
p1: Treaty condemned as a Diktat — Germany had no say in the negotiations led by Wilson, Clemenceau and Lloyd George.
p2: Signatories of the armistice accused of stabbing Germany in the back (Dolchstoss); called 'November Criminals'.
p3: Matthias Erzberger, who signed the armistice, was assassinated by a right-wing extremist in 1921.

Matthias Erzberger, who signed the armistice, was assassinated by a right-wing extremist in 1921.

front: What caused Hyperinflation?
p1: December 1922: Germany missed a reparations payment; France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr in retaliation.
p2: German government called a general strike in the Ruhr; loss of production → shortages and unemployment.
p3: Government printed money to pay striking workers → vicious cycle of inflation; bread: 1 mark (1919) → 200 billion marks (Nov 1923).
s: December 1922: Germany missed a reparations payment; France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr in retaliation.
German government called a general strike in the Ruhr; loss of production → shortages and unemployment.
Government printed money to pay striking workers → vicious cycle of inflation; bread: 1 mark (1919) → 200 billion marks (Nov 1923).

front: What was the impact of Hyperinflation?
p1: Collapse of society; mass shortages as foreign suppliers refused to accept German marks. People cannot afford basic goods.
p2: Middle-class savings wiped out overnight. Pensions also become worthless.
p3: Loss of trust in the Weimar government, which was seen as unable to manage the economy. Hitler attempted Munich Putsch during Hyperinflation.
s: Collapse of society; mass shortages as foreign suppliers refused to accept German marks. People cannot afford basic goods.
Middle-class savings wiped out overnight. Pensions also become worthless.
Loss of trust in the Weimar government, which was seen as unable to manage the economy. Hitler attempted Munich Putsch during Hyperinflation.

front: How did Stresemann stabilise Germany's economy?
p1: 1923: Rentenmark introduced to replace the worthless mark and end hyperinflation. Later strengthened to Reichsmark.
p2: 1924: Dawes Plan — reparations reduced to £50 million/year; $200 million US loans secured; Weimar recovery begins.
p3: 1929: Young Plan reduced total reparations to £2 billion and extended the deadline to 1988.

1929: Young Plan reduced total reparations to £2 billion and extended the deadline to 1988.

front: How did Stresemann improve Germany's foreign relations?
p1: 1925: Locarno Pact — France left the Ruhr; improved relations with Britain and France.
p2: 1926: Germany admitted to the League of Nations — accepted back into the international community.
p3: 1928: Kellogg-Briand Pact — 61 nations agreed to renounce war as a tool of foreign policy.

1928: Kellogg-Briand Pact — 61 nations agreed to renounce war as a tool of foreign policy.

front: How stable was the Weimar Republic between 1924–1928?
p1: Support for extremist parties dropped from 40% in 1924 to 28% in 1928 as the economy recovered — Nazis won only 12 seats in 1928.
p2: Election of war hero Paul von Hindenburg as President in 1925 increased nationalist support for the republic.
p3: But German economy dangerously reliant on American loans; underlying mistrust of government remained.

Election of war hero Paul von Hindenburg as President in 1925 increased nationalist support for the republic.

front: How did life change for workers in Weimar Germany?
p1: Unemployment benefit and sickness benefit introduced for the first time in 1927.
p2: Average working week fell from 50 to 46 hours; wages rose 25% by late 1920s.
p3: Government built 100,000 new homes to ease housing shortage; 4% unemployment rate by 1924.
s: Unemployment benefit and sickness benefit introduced for the first time in 1927.
Average working week fell from 50 to 46 hours; wages rose 25% by late 1920s.
Government built 100,000 new homes to ease housing shortage; 4% unemployment rate by 1924.

front: How did life change for women in Weimar Germany?
p1: Women gained equal voting rights; made up 10% of the Reichstag.
p2: Some traditional male jobs opened to women; number of female doctors doubled to 5,000 by 1932.
p3: Women paid on average 33% less than men; the 'new woman' challenged gendered social norms.
s: Women gained equal voting rights; made up 10% of the Reichstag.
Some traditional male jobs opened to women; number of female doctors doubled to 5,000 by 1932.
Women paid on average 33% less than men; the 'new woman' challenged gendered social norms.

front: What was culture like in Weimar Germany?
p1: Berlin became the centre of European avant-garde art and culture in the 1920s.

p3: Art: Otto Dix painted expressionist works highly critical of German society.

front: How did Hitler join the Nazi Party?
p1: After WWI Hitler was employed as a military spy to investigate the German Workers' Party (DAP) in Munich — led by Anton Drexler with only 23 members.
p2: Hitler became attracted to the DAP's ideas and joined in 1919.
p3: Within two years Hitler had taken control of the DAP and transformed it into the Nazi Party (NSDAP).

p1: 25 Point Programme (1920): campaigned against Weimar politicians, democracy, Jews, Treaty of Versailles and capitalism.
p2: Created party structure: permanent Munich office, swastika logo, Volkischer Beobachter newspaper; brought in Hess, Göring, Streicher, Röhm.
p3: August 1921: formed the SA (Sturmabteilung) — brownshirted ex-soldiers who intimidated opposition with violence.

front: Why did Hitler attempt the Munich Putsch in 1923?
p1: Nazi Party had grown to 50,000 members by 1923; Hitler believed right-wing Bavarian politicians like von Kahr would support him.
p2: Inspired by Mussolini's fascist March on Rome in 1922; boosted by support of war hero Ludendorff.
p3: 1923 context: Ruhr occupation and hyperinflation made Weimar Republic deeply unpopular — moment seemed right.

front: What happened during the Munich Putsch?
p1: 8 November 1923: Hitler and 600 SA burst into a Munich beer hall, fired a gun, and announced his intention to march on Berlin.
p2: Ludendorff mistakenly allowed von Kahr to leave; Kahr alerted the government in Berlin.
p3: 9 November: army crushed the Putsch; 16 Nazis killed. Hitler arrested.

front: What was the aftermath of the Munich Putsch?
p1: Nazi Party and SA banned; Hitler sentenced to 5 years in Landsberg Castle (released after 9 months).
p2: Hitler used his defence speech to gain national publicity; wrote Mein Kampf in prison outlining Nazi ideology.
p3: Direct revolution had failed → decided to win power through elections instead.

front: How did the Nazis reorganise in the 1920s?
p1: Party ban lifted 1925; spread nationwide — each region (Gau) led by a Gauleiter.
p2: SA grew to 400,000 by 1930; Hitler established personal bodyguard (SS) led by Heinrich Himmler.

front: Why did the Nazis not gain much support in 1924–29?
p1: Stresemann's economic recovery restored faith in Weimar — only 2.6% of the vote in 1928.
p2: Germany's improved international standing (League of Nations, Locarno) cut support for nationalist parties.
p3: Election of war hero Hindenburg as President in 1925 → increased public trust in Weimar; even opponents of the republic more willing to support it.

front: What was the impact of the Wall St. Crash (1929) on Germany?
p1: Wall Street crashed — £14 billion lost in a single day; US loans recalled immediately; German banks collapsed and demanded businesses repay loans.
p2: Mass unemployment: 6 million unemployed by 1933 — 50% of all people aged 16–30.
p3: Savings lost in banking crisis; homelessness surged; 24% increase in theft in Berlin.

front: How did the Great Depression affect the Nazis?
p1: Nazis rose from 2.6% (1928) to 37% and 230 seats by July 1932; Hitler won 13 million votes in the 1932 presidential election — came second to Hindenburg.
p2: Economic desperation drove millions to extremist ideas - Weimar was failing to deal with the crisis so support for moderates collapsed.
p3: Communists (KPD) also became popular; terrified the wealthy middle class → many backed the Nazis as protection.

p1: Goebbels ran 120 newspapers; ensured Nazi message spread via radio and eye-catching posters across Germany.

front: Why did Hindenburg make Hitler Chancellor?
p1: Chancellor Brüning resigned May 1932; Hitler was head of largest party but Hindenburg refused to make him Chancellor.
p2: Hindenburg appointed von Papen and then von Schleicher - both failed to control Reichstag without Nazi support. Von Schleicher threatened military dictatorship.

p1: 27 February 1933: Reichstag set fire by Dutch communist Marinus van der Lubbe.

p3: Hitler used Enabling Act to ban Trade Unions, all other political parties and local governments (länder).

p1: Röhm commanded 3 million SA men loyal to him personally — a dangerous rival power base. Röhm publicly critical of Hitler.

p3: The violent SA made Nazis look like thugs; SS leaders Himmler and Heydrich resented Röhm and wanted him removed.

p1: 30 June 1934: Röhm and approximately 400 other critics within the Nazi Party were murdered.
p2: Other enemies are removed including Von Kahr and Strasser who had crossed Hitler in 1920s.
p3: After Night of Long Knives, no one else in Nazi party would dare oppose Hitler - creates deterrence.

p1: 2 August 1934: Hindenburg died aged 86.

p3: Army swore personal oath to Hitler, not the republic → power was now absolute.

p1: SS: 300,000 members led by Himmler. Had unlimited power. Sent opponents to Concentration Camps like Dachau.

p1: Reich Church (1936): Protestant pastors had to support Hitler's views; Mein Kampf and the Bible used in sermons; swastikas displayed in churches.

front: How did KdF, DAF, and SdA affect German workers?
p1: DAF (German Labour Front): replaced trade unions; workers lost right to negotiate pay; DAF could punish workers who disrupted production.
p2: KdF (Strength through Joy): 35 million members by 1936; provided cinema, sports, foreign travel; KdF Wagon promised workers a Volkswagen but money taken for rearmament.
p3: SdA (Beauty of Labour): improved workplace facilities → toilets, canteens, changing rooms; workers had to do the construction themselves.

front: What were Nazi beliefs about race?
p1: Eugenics: belief that humans should be selectively bred to produce the 'ideal' Aryan human — forced evolution.
p2: Racial Hygiene: belief in the superiority of the Aryan race; races should be kept separate.
p3: Anti-Semitism: long-established racist beliefs against Jews given legal force under the Nazis. Nazis believed Jewish politicians were behind Dolchstoss (incorrectly).

front: How did Jewish persecution increase before Kristallnacht?
p1: 1933: Jews banned from civil service and teaching; SA boycott of Jewish shops — Star of David and 'Jude' painted on businesses.
p2: 1935: Nuremberg Laws → stripped Jews of German citizenship; banned from marrying non-Jews; required to wear yellow star.

front: What happened on Kristallnacht?
p1: 9–10 November 1938: assassination of a German official in Paris → used as pretext for organised violence.
p2: Thousands of synagogues and Jewish businesses burned; over 100 Jews killed; 30,000 arrested and sent to concentration camps.

front: How were other groups (non-Jews) persecuted by the Nazis?
p1: Slavs taught as inferior race ('Untermenschen'); Roma people ('Gypsies') arrested from 1933, deprived of citizenship 1938, deported 1939.
p2: Homosexuals: 1935 — 4,000 imprisoned; voluntary castration encouraged.
p3: Disabled people: 1933 — all disabled people sterilised; 1939 — T4 euthanasia programme begins.

front: How were communism and capitalism different?
p1: Communism: the state owns all property and industry to ensure a fair share for every citizen; based on writings of Karl Marx.
p2: Capitalism: individuals are free to own property and businesses; competition in markets drives success.
p3: Communist countries had limited freedoms and no democracy. Capitalist countries had more freedom and democracy.

front: What was the Grand Alliance and the Tehran Conference?
p1: From 1941 USSR, USA and UK united against common enemy Nazism.
p2: Churchill feared world communism; Stalin resented UK/US delaying the second front until 1944 — leaving the USSR fighting alone for 4 years.
p3: Tehran 1943: focused on wartime strategy; vague agreement that Germany would remain weak after the war.

front: What was agreed at the Yalta Conference?
p1: February 1945 (Roosevelt, Stalin, Churchill): Germany and Berlin split into 4 zones; Germany to pay $20 billion reparations, half to USSR.
p2: Stalin promised Poland and Eastern Europe would hold free elections.
p3: Eastern Europe agreed as a Soviet 'sphere of influence' — though the exact meaning was left undefined.

front: What disagreements were there at Yalta?
p1: Poland: Stalin wanted a 'friendly' Polish government; Britain had gone to war to defend Polish independence and refused to give in.
p2: Reparations level disputed — Britain and America feared repeating the mistakes of Versailles.

front: Why was there more tension at the Potsdam Conference?
p1: Hitler's death removed the common enemy; Roosevelt's death replaced a cooperative president with the far more hostile Truman.

p3: USA's successful atomic bomb test increased tension; Truman timed the testing of the bomb to intimidate Stalin.

front: What was the impact of the first atomic bomb?
p1: 6 and 9 August 1945: atomic bombs destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki, killing hundreds of thousands.
p2: Ushered in the nuclear age → direct threat to the USSR, which could not yet compete.

front: How did Stalin create Satellite States?
p1: Red Army had liberated Eastern Europe from Nazi rule; Stalin turned these states into a 'buffer zone' to protect the USSR from future invasion.
p2: Red Army used salami tactics to remove opponents in Hungary, Poland, Romania, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia until they became communist one-party states.

front: What did the Long and Novikov Telegrams say?
p1: February 1946: Kennan (US ambassador in Moscow) sent 8,000-word Long Telegram — Stalin planned 'world communism', but would back down under pressure.
p2: September 1946: Novikov Telegram — reported USA was planning to use military to dominate the world; cooperation impossible since Roosevelt's death.
p3: Both telegrams hardened attitudes on each side and shaped Cold War strategy. contributed to Truman Doctrine.

front: What was the Truman Doctrine?
p1: 1947: Truman declared capitalism as the system of freedom and democracy; communism as repression and violence — a choice between good and evil.
p2: Pledged America would contain communism from spreading further — beginning with a $400 million aid package to Greece and Turkey.
p3: Triggered by Britain's inability to keep financing anti-communist fighters in Greece — USA accepted responsibility to halt the spread of communism.

front: What was the Marshall Plan?
p1: General Marshall toured Europe and saw widespread devastation; convinced Truman to launch $13 billion of aid — Britain and France received largest shares.
p2: Offered to USSR and satellite states but Stalin rejected it, calling it 'Dollar Imperialism'.
p3: British foreign secretary called it 'a lifeline to sinking men'; Europe now divided into two economic camps.

front: What was COMINFORM and COMECON?
p1: COMINFORM (1947): Communist Information Bureau — coordinated policies of communist parties across Soviet satellite states, increasing Soviet control.
p2: COMECON (1949): Council for Mutual Economic Assistance — Soviet equivalent of the Marshall Plan, binding satellite economies to the USSR.
p3: Both were Stalin's response to the Marshall Plan — Europe was now divided into two distinct economic and political blocs.

front: Why did Stalin blockade Berlin?
p1: Stalin feared the West was rebuilding their German zones to create a powerful Germany capable of invading the USSR again.
p2: 1947: US and UK merged zones into 'Bizonia'; March 1948 France joined to make 'Trizonia'; June 1948 the Deutschmark introduced without consulting Stalin.
p3: 24 June 1948: Stalin closed all road and rail links from West Germany to West Berlin — attempting to starve the West out.

front: What was the impact of the Berlin Airlift?
p1: West airlifted 4,000 tonnes of food and fuel daily into West Berlin for 10 months. Stalin could not shoot down the planes without risking nuclear war.
p2: Huge propaganda victory for the West — demonstrated capitalism's commitment to its people.
p3: Cemented division of Germany (FRG and GDR established 1949); → NATO (1949) and Warsaw Pact (1955); USSR developed own nuclear bomb 1949.

p1: NATO (1949): USA, Britain, France and 9 others — if any member attacked, all would retaliate; → US military bases across Europe.

p3: Warsaw Pact (1955): Soviet equivalent with USSR and satellite states; commanded by Soviet Union — increased confrontation and risk of conflict.

front: How did the arms race develop 1945–60?
p1: 1945: USA develops A-bomb. 1949: USSR develops A-bomb. 1952: USA develops H-bomb (1,000× more powerful than Hiroshima). 1953: USSR develops its own.
p2: 1957: USA develops ICBM (fires nuclear bomb 4,500km). USSR develops it months later.

front: What was the space race?
p1: 1957: USSR launched Sputnik — first satellite. Seen as a military threat; USSR also sent dog Laika into space on Sputnik 2.
p2: 1961: USSR sent Yuri Gagarin into orbit — first man in space.
p3: Space race was a propaganda competition as well as a military one — showing whose system was more technologically advanced.

front: What was De-Stalinisation?
p1: 1953: Stalin died; two-year power struggle resulted in Nikita Khrushchev becoming leader in 1955.
p2: Khrushchev's secret speech: condemned Stalin's purges and cult of personality; old communists had heart attacks!.
p3: Khrushchev announced 'peaceful coexistence' with the West; maintained Soviet control of satellite states.

p1: Hungary's economy controlled by COMECON → prevented Marshall Aid or free trade with the West; forced to trade on uneven terms.
p2: Mátyás Rákosi was a brutal dictator who used the AVH secret police to maintain control — killed 2,000 people.

front: What happened during the Hungarian Uprising?
p1: Nagy replaced Rákosi; introduced reforms — ended one-party state, released political prisoners, remove Red Army. Khrushchev initially agreed.
p2: Nagy went too far: asked to leave Warsaw Pact. Khrushchev cannot accept. 1,000 tanks rolled into Budapest; 3,000 Hungarians killed, 20,000 fled.
p3: Nagy executed 1958; replaced by hard-line communist Kádár. America failed to help — would not intervene in the Soviet sphere.

front: Why did Khrushchev make his Berlin Ultimatum?
p1: 1950s: 3 million East Germans (1/5 of population) fled to the West through Berlin — 'Brain Drain' of skilled young workers.
p2: West Germany joined NATO in 1955 — confirming Soviet fears of a rearmed, threatening Germany.
p3: 1958 Berlin Ultimatum: West given 6 months to leave Berlin and declare it a 'free city', or Khrushchev would hand control of transport links to East Germany.

front: Why did the summits of 1959–61 fail to solve the Berlin Crisis?
p1: Geneva (May 1959) and Camp David (September 1959): little achieved, though Khrushchev postponed the six-month deadline.
p2: Paris Summit (1960): collapsed when Khrushchev demanded Eisenhower apologise for U2 spy plane incident; Eisenhower refused; Khrushchev stormed out.

front: What was the Berlin Wall?
p1: Refugee crisis intensified as East Germans feared the border would close — fled in their thousands. East German leader Ulbricht pleaded with Khrushchev to act.

p1: Khrushchev: refugee crisis halted; East economy could recover; communism survived in Berlin; Western spies could no longer easily cross.

front: What was the impact of the Cuban Revolution?
p1: New Year's Day 1959: Fidel Castro and Che Guevara overthrew the US-backed dictator Batista.
p2: Castro nationalised American land and companies; USA boycotted Cuban sugar; Castro turned to Khrushchev, who agreed to buy Cuban sugar.
p3: Cuba is 90 miles from USA. Became communist; seen as a direct threat to US security.

front: What was the Bay of Pigs invasion?
p1: 1961: Kennedy authorised the CIA to train 1,400 Cuban exiles to invade Cuba and overthrow Castro.

p1: 14 October 1962: Soviet missiles in Cuba spotted by a U2 spyplane. Kennedy convened ExComm to review options.

p3: Kennedy announced on television that any Soviet ship crossing the blockade would be fired upon — 13 days of crisis followed.

p1: Soviet ships sailed towards the blockade; the world held its breath. Letters exchanged between Kennedy and Khrushchev seeking a solution.

p1: 28 October 1962: America agreed to secretly remove its Jupiter missiles from Turkey and not invade Cuba.

front: What was the Prague Spring?
p1: Background: Czechoslovakia had been a democracy before WWII; Novotný's rule was deeply unpopular; economy run for benefit of USSR not Czechoslovakia.

p1: Brezhnev feared Czechoslovakia was becoming too capitalist and Soviet control would weaken.

p1: August 1968: USSR, Poland, Hungary, Bulgaria and East Germany invaded with 500,000 troops.

p1: Justified invasion of Czechoslovakia: if any communist country showed signs of turning towards capitalism, all communist countries had a duty to force it back.

p3: Collapsed entirely with Soviet invasion of Afghanistan 1979 — détente ended; SALT II cancelled; Second Cold War began.

front: Why did the Mujahedeen emerge in Afghanistan?
p1: 1978: communist PDPA seized power in Afghanistan. Communists imprisoned, tortured and murdered religious leaders.
p2: Many Afghans rejected the communist government — its atheism directly conflicted with their Muslim faith so formed Mujahedeen.
p3: Partly inspired by Iranian revolution where fundamentalist Shia cleric had overthrown the US - backed monarchy.

Partly inspired by Iranian revolution where fundamentalist Shia cleric had overthrown the US - backed monarchy.

front: Why did the USSR invade Afghanistan?
p1: Mujahedeen were winning; Brezhnev feared this would inspire rebellion in the Muslim regions in the south of the USSR.
p2: Christmas Eve 1979: USSR invaded to prop up the communist government.
p3: Soviets killed the unpopular President Amin and replaced him with the more pro-Moscow but still unpopular Kamal.

front: What happened during the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan?
p1: 10-year war costing the USSR $8 billion per year; estimated 15,000 Soviet soldiers killed.
p2: Red Army ill-prepared for Afghan landscape; Mujahedeen fought an effective guerrilla war.
p3: War deeply unpopular at home in the USSR — compared by critics to America's Vietnam.

Red Army ill-prepared for Afghan landscape; Mujahedeen fought an effective guerrilla war.
War deeply unpopular at home in the USSR — compared by critics to America's Vietnam.

front: What was the impact of the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan?
p1: Carter alarmed by Soviet presence near the Persian Gulf (US oil interests); Carter Doctrine — America would use force to defend the Persian Gulf.
p2: Economic sanctions on USSR — end of grain trade; America funded and supplied weapons to the Mujahedeen.
p3: Olympic boycotts: USA refused 1980 Moscow Olympics; USSR refused 1984 Los Angeles Olympics. SALT II cancelled — détente officially dead.

Economic sanctions on USSR — end of grain trade; America funded and supplied weapons to the Mujahedeen.

front: How did Reagan increase Cold War tensions?
p1: Reagan called USSR an 'Evil Empire', 'focus of evil in the modern world', compared them to the Nazis.
p2: Reagan Doctrine: USA would fund and support anti-communist resistance groups worldwide (e.g. Nicaragua); invaded Grenada to topple communist regime 1983.
p3: Raised military spending by $1 trillion including SDI.

Raised military spending by $1 trillion including SDI.

front: What was Reagan's SDI?
p1: 1983: Strategic Defence Initiative ('Star Wars') — announced orbital laser system to shoot down Soviet missiles and undermine MAD.
p2: SDI terrified the USSR → drove Gorbachev's rise and New Thinking.
p3: Was actually a bluff — only in development; Reagan announced it as if it was ready.

SDI terrified the USSR → drove Gorbachev's rise and New Thinking.
Was actually a bluff — only in development; Reagan announced it as if it was ready.

front: Why did Gorbachev introduce New Thinking?
p1: Brezhnev's 'era of stagnation': Soviet economy failing; 40% of income spent on nuclear weapons; $8 billion/year on Afghanistan war with no results.
p2: 1986 Chernobyl nuclear meltdown cost $18 billion to contain; poor living standards → unrest in satellite states (e.g. Poland 1981).
p3: Gorbachev became leader 1985 → concluded radical reform was essential.

1986 Chernobyl nuclear meltdown cost $18 billion to contain; poor living standards → unrest in satellite states (e.g. Poland 1981).
Gorbachev became leader 1985 → concluded radical reform was essential.

front: What was New Thinking?
p1: Perestroika ('Restructuring'): individuals and foreigners could now invest in businesses; Soviet state retained control of key industries.
p2: Glasnost ('Openness'): greater freedom of speech and press; political prisoners released; citizens encouraged to discuss solutions to Soviet problems.
p3: 1988: Sinatra Doctrine replaced the Brezhnev Doctrine — satellite states free to 'go their own way'.

1988: Sinatra Doctrine replaced the Brezhnev Doctrine — satellite states free to 'go their own way'.

front: What was the INF Treaty?
p1: Washington 1987: Intermediate Range Nuclear Force Treaty signed by Reagan and Gorbachev.
p2: Agreed to destroy all intermediate-range nuclear missiles — first arms reduction since détente.
p3: Beginning of end of Cold War. Gorbachev later said he would never start a hot war.

Agreed to destroy all intermediate-range nuclear missiles — first arms reduction since détente.
Beginning of end of Cold War. Gorbachev later said he would never start a hot war.

front: What happened in Eastern Europe in 1989?
p1: Eastern Europeans saw glasnost/perestroika in the USSR and demanded the same; hard-line leaders like Honecker (East Germany) refused to reform.
p2: Poland abandoned communism June 1989 → Solidarity won elections; Gorbachev sent no tanks → other states followed rapidly.
p3: Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria, Romania all became capitalist by end of 1989; Romania involved violent revolution.

Poland abandoned communism June 1989 → Solidarity won elections; Gorbachev sent no tanks → other states followed rapidly.
Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria, Romania all became capitalist by end of 1989; Romania involved violent revolution.

front: What was the impact of the fall of the Berlin Wall?
p1: 9 November 1989: crowds gathered at the Wall; East German guards stood down; people tore it down.
p2: German families and friends reunited after 28 years of separation.
p3: Germany officially reunified October 1990; Warsaw Pact dissolved July 1991 — symbolised the end of the Cold War.

German families and friends reunited after 28 years of separation.
Germany officially reunified October 1990; Warsaw Pact dissolved July 1991 — symbolised the end of the Cold War.

front: How did Gorbachev lose control over the USSR?
p1: Gorbachev seen as a hero in the West (Nobel Peace Prize 1990) but regarded as weak in the USSR.
p2: Soviet republics saw how easily satellite states had gained independence. 1990: Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania declared independence.
p3: Boris Yeltsin, president of Russia (the largest republic), began openly defying Gorbachev in early 1991.

Boris Yeltsin, president of Russia (the largest republic), began openly defying Gorbachev in early 1991.

front: Why did the USSR collapse in 1991?
p1: August 1991: 8 hard-line communist leaders (Gang of 8) staged a coup, removing Gorbachev from power and abolishing Glasnost and Perestroika.
p2: Boris Yeltsin led resistance → Gang of 8 coup collapsed after 3 days; Gorbachev restored but Gorbachev's authority weakened.
p3: Christmas Day 1991: Gorbachev resigned and announced the breakup of the USSR to avoid civil war; Yeltsin became 1st president of capitalist Russia.

front: What was society like in Elizabethan England?
p1: Majority rural; high levels of poverty. Society was hierarchical — everyone expected to keep their place.
p2: Nobles (dukes/earls): most powerful below Elizabeth; owned huge land, could raise armies. Gentry: less wealthy landowners, often JPs.
p3: Peasants: vast majority; entirely powerless. Poorest are vagrants - wandering landless poor.
s: Majority rural; high levels of poverty. Society was hierarchical — everyone expected to keep their place.
Nobles (dukes/earls): most powerful below Elizabeth; owned huge land, could raise armies. Gentry: less wealthy landowners, often JPs.
Peasants: vast majority; entirely powerless. Poorest are vagrants - wandering landless poor.

front: What was the role of Parliament and the Privy Council?
p1: Privy Council: 19 key advisors including William Cecil, Robert Dudley and Francis Walsingham.
p2: Parliament: needed to approve taxation; Elizabeth reluctant to call it too often.
p3: Royal prerogative: Elizabeth alone decided foreign policy, religion, succession and marriage.
s: Privy Council: 19 key advisors including William Cecil, Robert Dudley and Francis Walsingham.
Parliament: needed to approve taxation; Elizabeth reluctant to call it too often.
Royal prerogative: Elizabeth alone decided foreign policy, religion, succession and marriage.

front: What are key differences between Protestantism and Catholicism?
p1: Catholics believe Pope is head or Church. Protestants do not follow Pope. Priests in Catholicism are special and have direct connection to God
p2: Catholic bibles and services in latin; Protestant Bibles and services in local language. Catholic churches much more ornate.
p3: Eucharist - Catholics believe bread and wine becomes flesh and blood of Christ by miracle (transubstantiation). Seen as symbolic by Protestants.
s: Catholics believe Pope is head or Church. Protestants do not follow Pope. Priests in Catholicism are special and have direct connection to God
Catholic bibles and services in latin; Protestant Bibles and services in local language. Catholic churches much more ornate.
Eucharist - Catholics believe bread and wine becomes flesh and blood of Christ by miracle (transubstantiation). Seen as symbolic by Protestants.

front: What was controversial about the marriage of Henry VIII and Elizabeth's mother?
p1: Henry VIII divorced Catherine of Aragon to marry Anne Boleyn (Elizabeth's mother) — the Pope had not sanctioned the divorce.
p2: Catholics therefore regarded the marriage as invalid and Elizabeth as illegitimate and unfit to be queen. Saw Mary, Queen of Scots as true monarch.
p3: Henry VIII himself declared Elizabeth illegitimate in the 2nd Act of Succession 1536 — though he reversed this in the 3rd Act 1543.

Catholics therefore regarded the marriage as invalid and Elizabeth as illegitimate and unfit to be queen. Saw Mary, Queen of Scots as true monarch.
Henry VIII himself declared Elizabeth illegitimate in the 2nd Act of Succession 1536 — though he reversed this in the 3rd Act 1543.

front: What were beliefs about female power in the 16th century?
p1: Society was highly patriarchal — it was widely believed women could not control men in government or lead an army.
p2: John Knox wrote 'The first blast of the trumpet against the monstrous regiment of women' claiming women ruling was 'the blind leading those who can see'.
p3: It was expected Elizabeth would marry; a Tudor wife was legally required to obey her husband — unacceptable for a monarch.

John Knox wrote 'The first blast of the trumpet against the monstrous regiment of women' claiming women ruling was 'the blind leading those who can see'.
It was expected Elizabeth would marry; a Tudor wife was legally required to obey her husband — unacceptable for a monarch.

front: What were relations between England and foreign powers like in 1558?
p1: Spain: most powerful country in the world under Philip II (former husband of Mary I); controlled the New World and the Netherlands.
p2: France: 2nd most powerful; England's traditional enemy; at war with England until 1559 Treaty of Cateau-Cambrésis (England lost Calais).
p3: Scotland: independent, ruled by Mary, Queen of Scots (in France married to Prince Francis); bound to France by the Auld Alliance.

Scotland: independent, ruled by Mary, Queen of Scots (in France married to Prince Francis); bound to France by the Auld Alliance.

front: What was the impact of the French war at the start of Elizabeth's reign?
p1: England at war with France when Elizabeth took the throne — she had inherited a debt of £227,000 from Mary I.
p2: 1559 Treaty of Cateau-Cambrésis: Elizabeth relinquished England's claim to Calais — a humiliation but ended the costly war.
p3: Crown lands sold to raise quick income; reduced the Crown's long-term revenues.

front: What were the religious divides in England in 1558?
p1: Henry VIII's break with Rome 1534 → 25 years of religious turmoil; Protestant under Edward VI, Catholic under Mary I.
p2: Mary I burned 284 Protestants at the stake; over 800 extreme Protestants fled to Europe. They returned as Puritans.
p3: Elizabeth inherited Catholic bishops and clergy from Mary I; majority of the population — especially in the North — were Catholic.
s: Henry VIII's break with Rome 1534 → 25 years of religious turmoil; Protestant under Edward VI, Catholic under Mary I.
Mary I burned 284 Protestants at the stake; over 800 extreme Protestants fled to Europe. They returned as Puritans.
Elizabeth inherited Catholic bishops and clergy from Mary I; majority of the population — especially in the North — were Catholic.

front: What was the Religious Settlement?
p1: Act of Supremacy: Elizabeth declared 'supreme governor' of the Church of England; all clergy and officials had to swear loyalty.
p2: Act of Uniformity: all churches had to use the English Book of Common Prayer; 1 shilling recusancy fine for not attending a licensed church.
p3: Royal Injunctions: Catholic pilgrimages and saints denounced; images and vestments allowed; all churches to hold an English Bible.

Act of Uniformity: all churches had to use the English Book of Common Prayer; 1 shilling recusancy fine for not attending a licensed church.
Royal Injunctions: Catholic pilgrimages and saints denounced; images and vestments allowed; all churches to hold an English Bible.

front: What was the role of the Church of England in society?
p1: Church attendance was compulsory — the Church reached into every community in England through its parish structure.
p2: Parish priests key communicators of royal policy → sermons spread government messages.
p3: Visitations enforced the Act of Uniformity — inspectors checked churches were following the settlement correctly.
s: Church attendance was compulsory — the Church reached into every community in England through its parish structure.
Parish priests key communicators of royal policy → sermons spread government messages.
Visitations enforced the Act of Uniformity — inspectors checked churches were following the settlement correctly.

front: Why did Puritans dislike the Religious Settlement?
p1: Objected to Catholic elements retained in the settlement: images, vestments, church hierarchy.
p2: Disliked the vague wording of the Book of Common Prayer — it left too much room for Catholic interpretation of the Eucharist.
p3: Wanted a more thoroughly Protestant settlement — direct line to God without priestly hierarchy.
s: Objected to Catholic elements retained in the settlement: images, vestments, church hierarchy.
Disliked the vague wording of the Book of Common Prayer — it left too much room for Catholic interpretation of the Eucharist.
Wanted a more thoroughly Protestant settlement — direct line to God without priestly hierarchy.

front: Were the Puritans a serious threat?
p1: Threat: support in Privy Council (Leicester, Walsingham); some became bishops; MPs Strickland and Cope pressed for reform in Parliament.
p2: Not a threat: tiny minority (a few thousand); no foreign support; no alternative monarch; deeply divided.
p3: Several Puritan MPs imprisoned for debating the Religious Settlement without Elizabeth's permission.

Not a threat: tiny minority (a few thousand); no foreign support; no alternative monarch; deeply divided.

front: What was the Crucifix Controversy?
p1: 1559–60: Puritans pressured Elizabeth to remove crucifixes from all churches.
p2: Elizabeth backed down → crucifixes removed from all churches.
p3: Elizabeth kept crucifixes in her own personal chapel → symbolic compromise.
s: 1559–60: Puritans pressured Elizabeth to remove crucifixes from all churches.
Elizabeth backed down → crucifixes removed from all churches.
Elizabeth kept crucifixes in her own personal chapel → symbolic compromise.

front: What was the Vestment Controversy?
p1: 1566: Archbishop Parker's Advertisements ordered all priests to wear the plain white surplice.
p2: 37 London ministers refused to comply → suspended from their roles.
p3: Most priests complied under pressure → Puritan win was partial; vestments kept.
s: 1566: Archbishop Parker's Advertisements ordered all priests to wear the plain white surplice.
37 London ministers refused to comply → suspended from their roles.
Most priests complied under pressure → Puritan win was partial; vestments kept.

front: Why did Catholics not rebel before 1568?
p1: Settlement was more acceptable than feared — Elizabeth's tolerance kept the peace; recusancy fines of 1 shilling were not devastating.
p2: Pope did not excommunicate Elizabeth until 1570 — 11 years for Catholics to adjust to the settlement.
p3: Philip II of Spain protected Elizabeth at first. Preferred a Protestant monarch to Mary, Queen of Scots who would be a French puppet.

Pope did not excommunicate Elizabeth until 1570 — 11 years for Catholics to adjust to the settlement.

front: Why was Mary, Queen of Scots a threat to Elizabeth 1558–68?
p1: Catholics viewed Mary as the true Queen of England — Elizabeth's illegitimacy in Catholic eyes made Mary the rightful heir.
p2: Mary's marriage to Lord Darnley strengthened her claim; their son James (b.1566) highlighted Elizabeth's lack of an heir.
p3: 1560: Treaty of Edinburgh → Scottish lords gave up Mary's claim to English throne; Mary refused to accept it.

front: Why did Mary, Queen of Scots come to England and what was the York Conference?
p1: 1567: Mary deposed → suspected of involvement in assassination of Lord Darnley.
p2: 1568: Mary fled to England seeking Elizabeth's aid → left Elizabeth with an impossible dilemma.
p3: York Conference → Elizabeth chose imprisonment; prevented Mary becoming a rallying point for Catholic invasion.
s: 1567: Mary deposed → suspected of involvement in assassination of Lord Darnley.
1568: Mary fled to England seeking Elizabeth's aid → left Elizabeth with an impossible dilemma.

front: Why did the Northern Earls rebel?
p1: Religion: Earls of Westmoreland and Northumberland wanted to restore Catholicism to England. Marched under Catholic banners.
p2: Politics: Neville and Percy families had lost centuries of power in the North, replaced by Protestants in the Council of the North.
p3: Opportunity: Mary, Queen of Scots had recently arrived in northern England so they had a perfect figure to rally around.

Politics: Neville and Percy families had lost centuries of power in the North, replaced by Protestants in the Council of the North.
Opportunity: Mary, Queen of Scots had recently arrived in northern England so they had a perfect figure to rally around.

front: Why did the Revolt of the Northern Earls fail?
p1: Earls called on Catholic nobles to join → none came; nobles preferred paying the recusancy fine.
p2: Foreign Spanish support didn't appear despite capture of Hartlepool. Papal excommunication came months too late.
p3: Elizabeth's army of 14,000 faced them; the earls fled to Scotland. 450 rebels executed; Northumberland's head displayed at York.

Foreign Spanish support didn't appear despite capture of Hartlepool. Papal excommunication came months too late.
Elizabeth's army of 14,000 faced them; the earls fled to Scotland. 450 rebels executed; Northumberland's head displayed at York.

front: How serious was Papal Excommunication?
p1: 1570: Pope Pius V excommunicated Elizabeth and released all Catholics from loyalty to her — making it a Catholic's duty to overthrow her.
p2: 1571: Elizabeth made it treason to possess or spread copies of the Papal Bull.
p3: In long term increased tensions with Catholic foreign powers like Spain and France.

1571: Elizabeth made it treason to possess or spread copies of the Papal Bull.

front: How did Walsingham's spies keep Elizabeth safe?
p1: Walsingham built network of spies across Europe → intercepted letters and infiltrated Catholic plots.
p2: Discovered the Ridolfi Plot (1571) and Throckmorton Plot (1583) before they could succeed. Plotters were tortured to reveal co-conspirators.
p3: In the Babington Plot, Walsingham deliberately let the plot run to obtain written evidence proving Mary, Queen of Scots' direct involvement.

front: What happened in the Ridolfi and Throckmorton Plots?
p1: Ridolfi Plot (1571): Pope's spy plots to kill Elizabeth and make Mary QoS queen with Duke of Norfolk; Duke of Norfolk executed.
p2: Throckmorton Plot (1583): French Catholic army led by Duke of Guise (Mary's cousin) to invade, free Mary; discovered by Walsingham.
p3: Cecil and Walsingham to agree the Bond of Association (1584): both determined that Mary Queen of Scots will be executed next time.

front: What happened in the Babington Plot?
p1: 1586: French and Spanish forces planned to invade England and free Mary. Walsingham discovered the plot early but let it continue.
p2: Walsingham intercepted letters until he found one from Mary directly encouraging the plot — conclusive proof of treason.
p3: Mary tried by parliament, found guilty of treason; Elizabeth delayed signing the death warrant.

front: What led to Mary, Queen of Scots' execution?
p1: Elizabeth reluctant to execute Mary → feared precedent that parliaments could execute monarchs.
p2: Cecil and Walsingham knew Armada was imminent → Mary as a Spanish pawn had to be removed.
p3: Elizabeth signed the death warrant but forbade its use; Cecil sent it in secret. February 1587: Mary executed at Fotheringhay Castle.

Cecil and Walsingham knew Armada was imminent → Mary as a Spanish pawn had to be removed.

front: Why did England and Spain become rivals?
p1: Religious rivalry; 1570 Papal excommunication; 1584 Treaty of Joinville — France and Spain pledged to destroy Protestantism.
p2: Commercial rivalry: English cloth trade collapse in 1550s forced merchants to seek new markets; Spanish controlled the most valuable New World trade routes.
p3: 1572: Drake captured £40,000 from Spanish Panama; £400,000 during circumnavigation 1577–80 → Elizabeth knighted Drake on the Golden Hind.

front: What was England's involvement in the Dutch Revolt?
p1: From 1566 Protestant Dutch revolted against Catholic Spanish rule; Large Spanish army in Netherlands to fight rebels was concerning to England.
p2: Elizabeth supplied weapons and money secretly — eager to keep Spain distracted and support fellow protestants.
p3: 1584: Dutch leader William of Orange assassinated; Elizabeth signed Treaty of Nonsuch (1585) committing 7,400 troops and £126,000/year.
s: From 1566 Protestant Dutch revolted against Catholic Spanish rule; Large Spanish army in Netherlands to fight rebels was concerning to England.
Elizabeth supplied weapons and money secretly — eager to keep Spain distracted and support fellow protestants.
1584: Dutch leader William of Orange assassinated; Elizabeth signed Treaty of Nonsuch (1585) committing 7,400 troops and £126,000/year.

front: What did Dudley do in the Netherlands?
p1: Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, led English army — accepted title of Governor-General of the Netherlands against Elizabeth's wishes.
p2: Lacked enough men, money or supplies to defeat Parma's superior force. Only managed to slow Parma's progress.
p3: Key success: prevented Parma capturing Ostend → Parma's troops could not board the Armada.
s: Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, led English army — accepted title of Governor-General of the Netherlands against Elizabeth's wishes.
Lacked enough men, money or supplies to defeat Parma's superior force. Only managed to slow Parma's progress.

front: What did Drake do at Cadiz?
p1: 1587: Walsingham's spies reported a great Armada being built at Cadiz. Drake sent to buy England time.
p2: Drake slipped into Cadiz on a moonless night with four ships; destroyed 30 Spanish ships and damaged more; destroyed food barrels.
p3: Drake raided Portugal; captured treasure ship worth £140,000 → bought England 12 months to prepare.

front: What was Philip II's plan for the Armada?
p1: Duke of Medina-Sidonia to sail 130 ships and 27,000 men to the Spanish Netherlands.
p2: Rendezvous with Duke of Parma and his 30,000 men; combined force to invade England and kill Elizabeth.
p3: Plan fatally dependent on Parma and the Armada meeting at exactly the right time.

Rendezvous with Duke of Parma and his 30,000 men; combined force to invade England and kill Elizabeth.

front: How did English tactics defeat the Armada?
p1: Drake's raid on Cadiz gained England 12 months to prepare — warning beacons built along the coast.
p2: English navy (Drake and Howard) chased the slow Armada up the Channel, harrying from long range.
p3: Fireships sent into Armada at Calais → Spanish fleet scattered; English victory next day at Gravelines (8 August).

front: How did Spanish poor planning defeat the Armada?
p1: Armada led by inexperienced Medina-Sidonia — first-choice commander Santa Cruz had died.
p2: Parma not in Calais on time; failure to capture deep-water port of Ostend meant boarding Parma's troops would have taken 3 days.
p3: Philip's orders didn't allow for improvisation. Spanish didn't take opportunity to destroy English navy trapped at Plymouth.

Parma not in Calais on time; failure to capture deep-water port of Ostend meant boarding Parma's troops would have taken 3 days.

front: How did wind and weather defeat the Armada?
p1: After Gravelines, wind blew Armada north around Scotland and Ireland → unfamiliar, rough seas.
p2: 40 ships shipwrecked in storms; fewer than 80 ships and fewer than 10,000 men returned to Spain.
p3: English galleons were faster and more manoeuvrable than Spanish transport ships — better suited to rough English waters.
s: After Gravelines, wind blew Armada north around Scotland and Ireland → unfamiliar, rough seas.
40 ships shipwrecked in storms; fewer than 80 ships and fewer than 10,000 men returned to Spain.
English galleons were faster and more manoeuvrable than Spanish transport ships — better suited to rough English waters.

front: How did the defeat of the Armada boost Elizabeth?
p1: Tilbury Speech: Elizabeth addressed her army in full armour aged 55: 'I have the heart and stomach of a king' — challenged gender expectations.
p2: Victory → suggested God was on Protestants' side; medal: 'God blew, and they were scattered'.
p3: Defeat of the most powerful nation in the world boosted English confidence to explore, trade and attack Spain. Armada bankrupted Philip.
s: Tilbury Speech: Elizabeth addressed her army in full armour aged 55: 'I have the heart and stomach of a king' — challenged gender expectations.
Victory → suggested God was on Protestants' side; medal: 'God blew, and they were scattered'.
Defeat of the most powerful nation in the world boosted English confidence to explore, trade and attack Spain. Armada bankrupted Philip.

front: What was education like in Elizabeth's reign?
p1: End of reign 30% of men, 10% of women were literate (up from 20% and 10%). 72 new Grammar Schools established for middle class boys.
p2: Nobility: sons learned Latin, Greek, history, philosophy, government, theology. Girls also educated — Elizabeth herself was highly educated.
p3: Working class: education not available; children worked from early age. Some poor boys attended grammar schools funded by wealthy donors.
s: End of reign 30% of men, 10% of women were literate (up from 20% and 10%). 72 new Grammar Schools established for middle class boys.
Nobility: sons learned Latin, Greek, history, philosophy, government, theology. Girls also educated — Elizabeth herself was highly educated.
Working class: education not available; children worked from early age. Some poor boys attended grammar schools funded by wealthy donors.

front: What were the leisure activities of the poor?
p1: Football: often → deaths — no rules.
p2: Hunting rabbit. Music heard at fairs, markets, pubs and church.
p3: Gambling on blood-sports was common including bear-baiting (chained bear fighting dogs) and cock-fighting.
s: Football: often → deaths — no rules.
Hunting rabbit. Music heard at fairs, markets, pubs and church.
Gambling on blood-sports was common including bear-baiting (chained bear fighting dogs) and cock-fighting.

front: What were the leisure activities of the rich?
p1: Hunting on horseback (male and female), hawking, fishing, fencing, real tennis, wrestling.
p2: Luxury goods like tobacco from the New World; employed household musicians.
p3: Literature and poetry — patronage of writers like Shakespeare.
s: Hunting on horseback (male and female), hawking, fishing, fencing, real tennis, wrestling.
Luxury goods like tobacco from the New World; employed household musicians.
Literature and poetry — patronage of writers like Shakespeare.

front: What was the Elizabethan Theatre like?
p1: Protestantism encouraged secular plays → replaced medieval Bible stories; theatres backed by nobles like Earl of Leicester.
p2: Open to all social classes — 1 penny for the pit. Wealthy would pay to be seated above the action for prestige.
p3: From 1572 all plays had to be approved by the Queen's official — some censorship. Puritans opposed theatre as sinful and satanic.
s: Protestantism encouraged secular plays → replaced medieval Bible stories; theatres backed by nobles like Earl of Leicester.
Open to all social classes — 1 penny for the pit. Wealthy would pay to be seated above the action for prestige.
From 1572 all plays had to be approved by the Queen's official — some censorship. Puritans opposed theatre as sinful and satanic.

front: How did population rise lead to poverty?
p1: Population grew by around 1/3 in Elizabeth's reign from 3 million to 4 million.
p2: More people meant greater demand for food and land— rising prices. Also greater supply of labour — employers could pay less.
p3: Combined effect of rising prices and falling wages created widespread poverty - a Malthusian crisis.
s: Population grew by around 1/3 in Elizabeth's reign from 3 million to 4 million.
More people meant greater demand for food and land— rising prices. Also greater supply of labour — employers could pay less.
Combined effect of rising prices and falling wages created widespread poverty - a Malthusian crisis.

front: How did enclosure lead to poverty?
p1: Enclosure: wealthy landowners claimed common farmland, hedged it and used it to graze sheep instead of growing crops.
p2: Poor labourers lost their land and income; food prices rose as less was being grown.
p3: In the east of England 70% of farmland became enclosed. Blamed for the increase in poverty.
s: Enclosure: wealthy landowners claimed common farmland, hedged it and used it to graze sheep instead of growing crops.
Poor labourers lost their land and income; food prices rose as less was being grown.
In the east of England 70% of farmland became enclosed. Blamed for the increase in poverty.

front: How did debasement lead to poverty?
p1: 16th century coinage was based on a specific amount of precious metal, usually silver, to determine value.
p2: During the 1540s the currency was debased — precious metal removed from coins to create more of them.
p3: Merchants lost confidence in the value of coinage so raised prices → inflation.
s: 16th century coinage was based on a specific amount of precious metal, usually silver, to determine value.
During the 1540s the currency was debased — precious metal removed from coins to create more of them.
Merchants lost confidence in the value of coinage so raised prices → inflation.

front: What were Elizabethan attitudes to the poor?
p1: Deserving (impotent) poor — old, sick, disabled — deserved help. Undeserving (able-bodied) poor — fit to work but unemployed — treated harshly.
p2: Puritans believed idleness was a sin; feared exaggerated numbers of vagabonds could stir revolts; blamed vagabonds for plague outbreaks.
p3: Vagabonds associated with crime — with little law enforcement, hostility was widespread.
s: Deserving (impotent) poor — old, sick, disabled — deserved help. Undeserving (able-bodied) poor — fit to work but unemployed — treated harshly.
Puritans believed idleness was a sin; feared exaggerated numbers of vagabonds could stir revolts; blamed vagabonds for plague outbreaks.
Vagabonds associated with crime — with little law enforcement, hostility was widespread.

front: How were the poor treated by new laws?
p1: Statute of Artificers (1563): established maximum national wages for specific jobs to deter economic migration.
p2: Vagabonds Act (1572): vagabonds over 14 whipped and burned through the right ear; later executed; government collected poor rate for deserving poor.
p3: Act for the Relief of the Poor (1576): towns required to find work for the undeserving poor; those refusing work sent to a House of Correction.
s: Statute of Artificers (1563): established maximum national wages for specific jobs to deter economic migration.
Vagabonds Act (1572): vagabonds over 14 whipped and burned through the right ear; later executed; government collected poor rate for deserving poor.
Act for the Relief of the Poor (1576): towns required to find work for the undeserving poor; those refusing work sent to a House of Correction.

front: What new technologies made it easier to explore?
p1: 1569 Mercator Map: new accurate world map made long-distance navigation safer.
p2: Astrolabe: allowed navigators to determine latitude by measuring the angle of the North Star.
p3: English galleons: faster and more manoeuvrable with greater cargo space; low bow and stern increased stability in ocean conditions.
s: 1569 Mercator Map: new accurate world map made long-distance navigation safer.
Astrolabe: allowed navigators to determine latitude by measuring the angle of the North Star.
English galleons: faster and more manoeuvrable with greater cargo space; low bow and stern increased stability in ocean conditions.

front: Why did Elizabethans explore?
p1: English wanted to plunder Spanish trade routes in New World and find new markets after the collapse of cloth trade in the 1550s.
p2: Financial gain and fame: Drake returned from circumnavigation with £400,000 of Spanish gold; new luxury goods (tobacco, cocoa, potatoes) for profit.
p3: 1562: Hawkins created Triangular Slave Trade → large wealth for England.
s: English wanted to plunder Spanish trade routes in New World and find new markets after the collapse of cloth trade in the 1550s.
Financial gain and fame: Drake returned from circumnavigation with £400,000 of Spanish gold; new luxury goods (tobacco, cocoa, potatoes) for profit.
1562: Hawkins created Triangular Slave Trade → large wealth for England.

front: What happened during Drake's Circumnavigation?
p1: 1577–80: Drake was raiding Spanish colonies in South America; pursued by Spanish ships so escaped into the Pacific.
p2: Returned with over £400,000 of Spanish gold (£500 million today); became 2nd person in history and 1st Englishman to circumnavigate the globe.
p3: Established a short-lived colony near San Francisco (Nova Albion); publicly knighted by Elizabeth on the deck of the Golden Hind 1581.
s: 1577–80: Drake was raiding Spanish colonies in South America; pursued by Spanish ships so escaped into the Pacific.
Returned with over £400,000 of Spanish gold (£500 million today); became 2nd person in history and 1st Englishman to circumnavigate the globe.
Established a short-lived colony near San Francisco (Nova Albion); publicly knighted by Elizabeth on the deck of the Golden Hind 1581.

front: What went wrong in the planning of the colony of Virginia?
p1: Poor leadership: Raleigh organised and financed the voyages but never went himself; Ralph Lane was too hot-headed to manage relations with Natives.
p2: All food stored on The Tiger → colony fatally vulnerable when it hit a reef; supplies destroyed by seawater.
p3: Wrong colonists sent: too many merchants, soldiers and craftsmen; almost no one who could farm the land or produce food for a long-term settlement.
s: Poor leadership: Raleigh organised and financed the voyages but never went himself; Ralph Lane was too hot-headed to manage relations with Natives.
All food stored on The Tiger → colony fatally vulnerable when it hit a reef; supplies destroyed by seawater.
Wrong colonists sent: too many merchants, soldiers and craftsmen; almost no one who could farm the land or produce food for a long-term settlement.

front: What happened at Roanoke Island?
p1: 1585: The Tiger hit a reef, destroying food supplies → colonists immediately dependent on the Algonquian.
p2: Relations deteriorated as disease spread to natives (invisible bullets); Lane massacred Wingina's village and decapitated him. Colony abandoned.
p3: 1587 (second colony): new settlers arrived too late to plant crops; Attacked by native forces; Armada prevented supply ships; Colony disappeared.
s: 1585: The Tiger hit a reef, destroying food supplies → colonists immediately dependent on the Algonquian.
Relations deteriorated as disease spread to natives (invisible bullets); Lane massacred Wingina's village and decapitated him. Colony abandoned.
1587 (second colony): new settlers arrived too late to plant crops; Attacked by native forces; Armada prevented supply ships; Colony disappeared.

front: What was England like in the Medieval period?
p1: Majority rural society; most people were peasants farming the land with little power or wealth. Cloth trade became important later in the period.
p2: Kings had complete power and there was no parliament. Weak defences meant that invasions were common.
p3: Religion dominated life — the Church was central to government, law and culture. Monasteries were wealthy and poorly defended.
s: Majority rural society; most people were peasants farming the land with little power or wealth. Cloth trade became important later in the period.
Kings had complete power and there was no parliament. Weak defences meant that invasions were common.
Religion dominated life — the Church was central to government, law and culture. Monasteries were wealthy and poorly defended.

front: Why did the Vikings come to England?
p1: Economic: Vikings came to trade and later to raid, attracted by England's wealth and weak coastal defences compared to scarce resources in Scandinavia.
p2: War: 865 — Great Heathen Army invaded seeking revenge for the murder of Ragnar Lodbrok by King Ælla of Northumbria.
p3: Religion: Norse religion believed the only way to Valhalla (paradise) was to die in battle. Motivated exploration and conquest.
s: Economic: Vikings came to trade and later to raid, attracted by England's wealth and weak coastal defences compared to scarce resources in Scandinavia.
War: 865 — Great Heathen Army invaded seeking revenge for the murder of Ragnar Lodbrok by King Ælla of Northumbria.
Religion: Norse religion believed the only way to Valhalla (paradise) was to die in battle. Motivated exploration and conquest.

front: What was the Viking experience in the Danelaw?
p1: 878: Treaty between Alfred and Guthrum — Vikings allowed to settle in Danelaw (northeastern England); many assimilated and converted to Christianity.
p2: Vikings faced hostility: 1002 — King Æthelred ordered the St Brice's Day Massacre — death of all Danes in England. It is not known how many were killed.
p3: 1016: Cnut → Viking king of all England; kept English laws; promoted assimilation with English population.
s: 878: Treaty between Alfred and Guthrum — Vikings allowed to settle in Danelaw (northeastern England); many assimilated and converted to Christianity.
Vikings faced hostility: 1002 — King Æthelred ordered the St Brice's Day Massacre — death of all Danes in England. It is not known how many were killed.
1016: Cnut → Viking king of all England; kept English laws; promoted assimilation with English population.

front: How did the Vikings impact England?
p1: Built Environment: Vikings built burhs (fortified towns) across England. They grew into Nottingham, Leicester, and Derby.
p2: Government: Vikings introduced 'Things' — local democratic assemblies where communities voted on laws and decided guilt (early juries).
p3: Language: Old Norse heavily influenced English; Over 1,000 words including egg and knife; days of the week (e.g. Thursday = Thor's day).
s: Built Environment: Vikings built burhs (fortified towns) across England. They grew into Nottingham, Leicester, and Derby.
Government: Vikings introduced 'Things' — local democratic assemblies where communities voted on laws and decided guilt (early juries).
Language: Old Norse heavily influenced English; Over 1,000 words including egg and knife; days of the week (e.g. Thursday = Thor's day).

front: Case Study: York under the Vikings
p1: York (Jorvik) grew from a town of 1,000 in 850 to a city of around 15,000 people by 950 — one of the largest cities in England.
p2: Became an international trading hub with rivers Ouse and Foss linking Jorvik to the sea. Goods traded from Africa and Constantinople (Istanbul).
p3: Evidence of peaceful co-operation and assimilation between English Christians and Vikings.
s: York (Jorvik) grew from a town of 1,000 in 850 to a city of around 15,000 people by 950 — one of the largest cities in England.
Became an international trading hub with rivers Ouse and Foss linking Jorvik to the sea. Goods traded from Africa and Constantinople (Istanbul).
Evidence of peaceful co-operation and assimilation between English Christians and Vikings.

front: Why did Normans invade England in 1066?
p1: King Edward the Confessor died without children; William, Duke of Normandy claimed Edward had named him as heir. Invaded to assert his claim.
p2: William promised any Norman knight who supported the invasion land and power in England. Thousands followed William.
p3: Pope supported the invasion → gave religious legitimacy; William carried a Papal banner at Hastings.
s: King Edward the Confessor died without children; William, Duke of Normandy claimed Edward had named him as heir. Invaded to assert his claim.
William promised any Norman knight who supported the invasion land and power in England. Thousands followed William.
Pope supported the invasion → gave religious legitimacy; William carried a Papal banner at Hastings.

front: What was life like for the Normans after 1066?
p1: Normans became the ruling class — given land and positions at the top of the Feudal System by William. 200 Norman barons owned majority of English land.
p2: English rebellions 1069-70 → Normans increased oppression and control. Responded with brutal Harrying of North.
p3: French was the official language of England for 200 years after 1066 — though the poor continued to speak English. Limited assimilation.
s: Normans became the ruling class — given land and positions at the top of the Feudal System by William. 200 Norman barons owned majority of English land.
English rebellions 1069-70 → Normans increased oppression and control. Responded with brutal Harrying of North.
French was the official language of England for 200 years after 1066 — though the poor continued to speak English. Limited assimilation.

front: How did the Normans impact England?
p1: Feudal System: imposed a strict hierarchy — King, barons, knights, English peasants at the bottom. The Normans formed the ruling class for centuries.
p2: Built environment: hundreds of castles and cathedrals built to dominate England. Tower of London (1070) built to control Londoners.
p3: French became language of power - 'parliament'; French words used for food e.g. 'Boeuf'; English names (Athelstan) replaced with William, Henry, Robert etc.
s: Feudal System: imposed a strict hierarchy — King, barons, knights, English peasants at the bottom. The Normans formed the ruling class for centuries.
Built environment: hundreds of castles and cathedrals built to dominate England. Tower of London (1070) built to control Londoners.
French became language of power - 'parliament'; French words used for food e.g. 'Boeuf'; English names (Athelstan) replaced with William, Henry, Robert etc.

front: Why did the English Kings protect Jewish moneylenders?
p1: 1070: William I invited Jewish moneylenders to England — Papal ban on usury (charging interest) meant only Jews could legally lend money at interest.
p2: Kings relied on Jewish loans to fund castles, wars and government — 8% of royal income came from Jewish communities.
p3: 1135: Royal Charter granted liberties to Jews; Jewries (Jewish communities) developed across England. Jews could swear oaths on Torah and received fair trials.
s: 1070: William I invited Jewish moneylenders to England — Papal ban on usury (charging interest) meant only Jews could legally lend money at interest.
Kings relied on Jewish loans to fund castles, wars and government — 8% of royal income came from Jewish communities.
1135: Royal Charter granted liberties to Jews; Jewries (Jewish communities) developed across England. Jews could swear oaths on Torah and received fair trials.

front: Why did people's attitudes to Jews in medieval England change?
p1: Crusades → priests condemned non-Christians → Jewish communities targeted.
p2: 1144: First blood libel stories emerged in Norwich — Jews falsely accused of murdering Christian children for rituals.
p3: 1189–90: Large-scale anti-Semitic riots across England; March 1190: 150 Jews committed suicide in York Castle to avoid mass baptism.
s: Crusades → priests condemned non-Christians → Jewish communities targeted.
1144: First blood libel stories emerged in Norwich — Jews falsely accused of murdering Christian children for rituals.

front: How did royal treatment of Medieval Jews worsen?
p1: 1200s: Henry III introduced restrictions — Tabula (yellow badge) enforced; Jewish community increasingly scapegoated and taxation increased.
p2: 1265: Pope allowed Christians to perform usury - meant that Kings no longer needed Jewish moneylenders for finance.
p3: 1275: Statute of Jewry banned Jews from usury; 1290: Edward I expelled all Jews → over 3,000 forced into exile.
s: 1200s: Henry III introduced restrictions — Tabula (yellow badge) enforced; Jewish community increasingly scapegoated and taxation increased.
1265: Pope allowed Christians to perform usury - meant that Kings no longer needed Jewish moneylenders for finance.
1275: Statute of Jewry banned Jews from usury; 1290: Edward I expelled all Jews → over 3,000 forced into exile.

front: What was the impact of Medieval Jewish communities?
p1: Jewish loans funded major building projects including 84 Norman castles and royal government.
p2: 8% of royal income came from Jewish communities — crucial to English state finances.
p3: Jacob of Oxford, a Jewish moneylender, helped to fund and develop the University of Oxford.
s: Jewish loans funded major building projects including 84 Norman castles and royal government.
8% of royal income came from Jewish communities — crucial to English state finances.
Jacob of Oxford, a Jewish moneylender, helped to fund and develop the University of Oxford.

front: Why did European traders and craftsmen come to England?
p1: 14th–15th centuries: cloth trade highly profitable → Flemish weavers and Hansa merchants came to profit.
p2: 1351: Edward III invited Flemish weavers to develop the cloth trade after they were evicted from their French hometowns during the Hundred Years' War.
p3: 1303: Edward I gave Hansa merchants permission to establish the Steelyard in London — trading wool and cloth to Northern Europe.
s: 14th–15th centuries: cloth trade highly profitable → Flemish weavers and Hansa merchants came to profit.

1303: Edward I gave Hansa merchants permission to establish the Steelyard in London — trading wool and cloth to Northern Europe.

front: What was the experience of European traders and craftsmen?
p1: Normally lived in harmony with English neighbours during prosperous times. Could apply for Denizen status from 1378 and had right to fair trial.
p2: 1381: foreign merchants attacked during the Peasants' Revolt — 150 murdered.
p3: Craft guilds resented migrants as job competition — especially hostile to Flemish weavers; 1440: alien taxes introduced.

front: What was the impact of European traders and craftsmen?
p1: Flemish weavers transformed Colchester — from the 53rd to the 13th richest town in England.
p2: Hansa merchants helped make the wool trade extremely profitable; the Steelyard became a major trading base in London.
p3: European craftsmen introduced new weaving, metalwork and trade techniques → wool trade profits rose across England.
s: Flemish weavers transformed Colchester — from the 53rd to the 13th richest town in England.
Hansa merchants helped make the wool trade extremely profitable; the Steelyard became a major trading base in London.
European craftsmen introduced new weaving, metalwork and trade techniques → wool trade profits rose across England.

front: How did England change in the Early Modern period?
p1: In 1500s England became a predominately Protestant nation under Henry VIII, Edward VI and Elizabeth I. Europe is divided between Protestants and Catholics.
p2: In the 1600s the Civil War between Parliament and King → growth in Parliament; decrease in royal power by end of the period.
p3: This period saw the beginnings of empire with early colonies in America and India and the beginning of Britain's involvement in the slave trade.
s: In 1500s England became a predominately Protestant nation under Henry VIII, Edward VI and Elizabeth I. Europe is divided between Protestants and Catholics.
In the 1600s the Civil War between Parliament and King → growth in Parliament; decrease in royal power by end of the period.
This period saw the beginnings of empire with early colonies in America and India and the beginning of Britain's involvement in the slave trade.

front: Why did the Huguenots come to England?
p1: Huguenots were French Protestants fleeing Catholic persecution — St Bartholomew's Day Massacre (1572) killed 30,000 Huguenots in France.
p2: Second wave of 50,000 Huguenots arrive in 1680s after French Kings resume persecution of Protestants. All Huguenots offered Denizen status by King Charles II.
p3: Government actively welcomes and encourages Huguenot migration as they know the positive impact they can have on the economy.
s: Huguenots were French Protestants fleeing Catholic persecution — St Bartholomew's Day Massacre (1572) killed 30,000 Huguenots in France.
Second wave of 50,000 Huguenots arrive in 1680s after French Kings resume persecution of Protestants. All Huguenots offered Denizen status by King Charles II.
Government actively welcomes and encourages Huguenot migration as they know the positive impact they can have on the economy.

front: What was the experience of Huguenot migrants?
p1: 1681: Charles II granted Denizen status → legal protection and residency rights.
p2: 1680s: tensions in Spitalfields between Huguenots and English workers who accused them of stealing jobs.
p3: 1600s: many English people donated money to help Huguenots settle — viewed with sympathy as Protestant victims of persecution.

front: What was the impact of Huguenot migrants?
p1: Economy: Helped found the Bank of England in 1694; started the English paper industry — 200 paper mills by 1714.
p2: Built Environment Transformed Spitalfields into a prosperous weaver town; cloth exports were 20 times higher by the end of the 17th century.
p3: Huguenot scientists contributed to development of inoculations; 2/3 of printers in England were European migrants.
s: Economy: Helped found the Bank of England in 1694; started the English paper industry — 200 paper mills by 1714.
Built Environment Transformed Spitalfields into a prosperous weaver town; cloth exports were 20 times higher by the end of the 17th century.

front: Case Study: Flemish migrants in Sandwich
p1: 1561: local government of Sandwich invited Flemish weavers to support the local economy following the Dutch Revolt.
p2: 400 Flemings settled in Sandwich - boosted weaving economy. Ships in the town's harbour trebled over next decade.
p3: Increasing restrictions and hostility as Flemish migrants were accused of 'taking English jobs'; Flemish banned from non-weaving jobs.

front: Case Study: Walloon migrants in Canterbury
p1: 1570s: local government of Canterbury invited Walloon migrants (French-speaking Protestants from the Netherlands) to boost the local economy.
p2: Walloons became highly successful → employed English people; taught skills; Canterbury became prosperous.
p3: 1580s: Walloons seen as a positive influence in Canterbury — by developing and teaching new trades including diamond cutting and sugar refining.
s: 1570s: local government of Canterbury invited Walloon migrants (French-speaking Protestants from the Netherlands) to boost the local economy.
Walloons became highly successful → employed English people; taught skills; Canterbury became prosperous.

front: Why did Oliver Cromwell allow Jewish migrants to return to England in 1656?
p1: Rabbi Manasseh ben Israel campaigned for their return — as Jews were facing intense violence in other European countries.
p2: Cromwell's Puritan beliefs led him to allow their return so they could be converted to Christianity.
p3: Pragmatic reasons: Jewish financiers would help turn London into a major financial centre; Cromwell was aware of their contribution to the Dutch economy.

Cromwell's Puritan beliefs led him to allow their return so they could be converted to Christianity.

front: What was the experience of Jewish migrants in the Early Modern period?
p1: 1656: allowed to build their own synagogue; but restricted — forbidden from attending university, serving in the army or becoming lawyers or MPs.
p2: Late 1600s: Jewish community in London had a positive relationship with the mayor and people of the city. But anti-Semitic stereotypes continued.
p3: After 1656, Jewish financiers → London became a major financial centre.
