Late 1600s: Jewish community in London had a positive relationship with the mayor and people of the city. But anti-Semitic stereotypes continued.

front: How did the experience of black people in England change in the Early Modern period?
p1: Early 1500s: evidence of black Africans living peacefully alongside the English population e.g. John Blanke — successful black trumpeter.
p2: From the 1560s: Elizabeth I sponsored John Hawkins and Francis Drake in the slave trade; black people began to be seen as property.
p3: 1660: King Charles II founded Royal African Company to enslave West Africans. Ultimately responsible for enslaving c.200,000 Africans.

front: Why did Palatines come to England?
p1: 17th Century: Wars in the Rhineland → instability; approximately 13,000 Protestant Palatine refugees sought refuge in England.
p2: 1708–09: Parliament passed the Foreign Protestants Naturalisation Act — offering citizenship to all foreign Protestants.
p3: Palatines hoping to travel from England on to the Carolina colonies in America.
s: 1708–09: Wars in the Rhineland → instability; approximately 13,000 Protestant Palatine refugees sought refuge in England.
1708–09: Parliament passed the Foreign Protestants Naturalisation Act — offering citizenship to all foreign Protestants.
Palatines hoping to travel from England on to the Carolina colonies in America.

front: What was the experience of Palatine migrants?
p1: Palatines were mainly farmers with few specialist skills → seen as an economic burden.
p2: Huge refugee camps emerged outside London as Palatines arrived. Many British saw them as a threat - not people to welcome.
p3: 3,000 Palatines deported to Ireland 1709 when numbers overwhelmed London.

front: How did Britain change in the 18th and 19th centuries?
p1: Industrial Revolution: Britain became 'workshop of the world'; huge demand for labour in new industrial port cities like Glasgow and Liverpool.
p2: British Empire conquered ¼ of the globe including India, the Caribbean and parts of Africa — increased migration between colonies and Britain.
p3: Civil Liberties developed in this period including increased democracy, freedoms of speech, and increased tolerance of religion.
s: Industrial Revolution: Britain became 'workshop of the world'; huge demand for labour in new industrial port cities like Glasgow and Liverpool.
British Empire conquered ¼ of the globe including India, the Caribbean and parts of Africa — increased migration between colonies and Britain.

front: Why did Irish migrants come to Britain in the 1840s?
p1: 1845–46: Potato Blight → famine; approximately 2 million fled Ireland; 1 million died.
p2: Ireland lacked industrial cities → economic migration to British industrial cities for factory and construction work.
p3: Protestant minority (10%) owned 86% of the land; Catholic majority (90% of population) owned just 14% — despite Catholic Emancipation 1829, land stayed in Protestant hands.

p1: Worked harsh conditions as 'Navvies' — building Britain's canals and railways. Blamed by the media for diseases and lowering wages.

p1: Irish Navvies built the rail network connecting all cities and ports in Britain — transformed trade and communication.

front: Why did Asian migrants come to Britain in the 18th and 19th centuries?
p1: East Indian Company (EIC) took control over India. EIC elite employed Indian nannies (Ayahs) and often brought them back to England.

p1: Sake Dean Mohamed opened the first curry house in England in 1810 — one of the earliest examples of South Asian cultural impact.

p1: Liverpool's ports made it central to migration. Irish and Lascar communities developed working on docks.

front: How did the experience of black people in Britain change in the 18th and 19th centuries?
p1: 1700s: Slavery at its height. African 'servants' in Britain likely to be enslaved. African child servants seen as status symbols.

p1: Olaudah Equiano and Ignatius Sancho wrote autobiographies that helped persuade the public and MPs to abolish slavery.

front: Why did 150,000 Ashkenazi Jews come to Britain in the 1880s?
p1: 1880s: violent pogroms in Russian Empire → ~150,000 Ashkenazi Jews fled to Britain.

p1: Settled in Whitechapel — many only spoke Yiddish and worked in harsh textile sweatshops.

front: How did Britain change in the Modern period?
p1: WWI (1914–18) and WWII (1939–45): millions of colonial soldiers from Africa, India and the Caribbean fought for Britain.
p2: WWII: British Empire decolonised → mass migration. Replaced by Commonwealth. Britain joined European Union.
p3: After WWII, British economy including NHS and transport became reliant on migrant labour.

front: What was the experience of refugees to Britain?
p1: Belgian refugees in WWI; Polish refugees in WWII — 1947 Polish Resettlement Act allowed those who had served in the British military to remain.

front: How did WWI (1914-18) affect migration?
p1: Millions of colonial soldiers from Africa, India and the Caribbean served in the British armed forces.

front: How did WWII (1939-45) affect migration?
p1: Millions of colonial soldiers fought for Britain → increased connection between Britain and Commonwealth.

front: Why did the Windrush Generation come to Britain?
p1: Post-WWII: Britain needed rebuilding → huge recruitment drives by London Transport and NHS in the Caribbean.

front: How did laws about who could migrate to Britain change in the 20th century?
p1: 1905 Aliens Act: first restriction on migration — targeted 'undesirable' (mainly Jewish) migrants.

front: What was the experience of Windrush migrants?
p1: Colour bars common in housing and employment: 'No Blacks, No Dogs, No Irish' signs. White-dominated trade unions viewed migrants as threats.
p2: 1958: race riots in Nottingham and Notting Hill. 1968: Enoch Powell's 'Rivers of Blood' speech — 74% of the public agreed with him.

front: How did Windrush migrants impact Britain?
p1: Windrush Generation rebuilt post-war Britain → by 1960s, 12% of London Transport from ethnic minorities; by 2003, 30% of NHS doctors and 44% of nurses were migrants.

front: What were the anti-immigrant political movements of the 20th century?
p1: 1936: Battle of Cable Street - Oswald Mosley's blackshirts tried an intimidatory march through Jewish Whitechapel - locals resisted.

p1: 60,000 East African Asian migrants settled in Leicester in 1960s–70s despite council advert in Ugandan newspapers deterring migration.

p1: Victorian houses subdivided into cramped, expensive bedsits. Slum landlords like Peter Rachman charged high rents and provided poor conditions.
p2: Migrants typically lived in Homes of Multiple Occupancy (HMOs). Multiple tenants — trapped in overcrowded, poor-quality accommodation.

p1: Notting Hill Housing Trust set up by Bruce Kenrick to provide better affordable housing for the Caribbean community..

p1: Shebeens were unlicensed clubs run in private houses by Caribbean migrants — provided music, food and drink in a welcoming community space.

p3: Police regularly raided shebeens — another flashpoint between the Caribbean community and the Metropolitan Police.

p1: Mangrove on All Saints Road was a Caribbean restaurant and community hub run by Frank Crichlow — black celebrities like Hendrix, Marley and Ross ate there.

p1: White Teddy Boys and far-right groups launched violent attacks on Black residents over several nights — targeting mixed race couples.
